answer_text:
# 💜 The History of Purple

---

## A Colour Born from the Sea

Every great story has an unlikely beginning, and purple's begins with a dog on a beach.

Tyrian purple dye was first manufactured by the Phoenicians in the 16th century BCE. According to legend recorded by the Greek scholar Julius Pollux in the 2nd century CE, the dye was discovered by the Phoenician god Melqart while walking along the seashore with his dog and the nymph Tyros. When the dog returned, his muzzle was stained violet. When Melqart looked closer, he found in the dog's teeth a crushed sea snail, oozing and purple. Immediately smitten with the colour, Tyros agreed to marry Melqart if he could fashion her a robe in the same vibrant hue. Determined and resourceful, Melqart collected enough sea snails to fulfil the wish of his beloved — and thus "Tyrian purple" and the Phoenician trade in textiles was born.

---

## The World's Most Expensive Colour

The name Phoenicia, translated from the Greek as "purple land," shows the deep connection between the area — now modern-day Lebanon — and its history of dye production. Phoenicia was the birthplace of purple dye, first recorded in the 14th century BCE and made from the glands of shellfish.

The reality of making this dye was far from the romance of the myth. To produce the dye, ancient people collected thousands of murex sea snails along the beach — species like *Hexaplex trunculus*, *Bolinus brandaris*, and *Stramonita haemastoma*, each of which produced a slightly different shade — and either crushed the snails whole or cut out their tiny mucous glands. Dyeing with murex was a complex process involving extracting the liquid while the mollusc was still alive and exposing it to sunlight for a specified period of time, during which the dye changed colour. It could take up to 12,000 molluscs to produce just one gram of dye.

It is believed that the intensity of the purple hue improved rather than faded as the dyed cloth aged — a remarkable and coveted quality in a world where most natural dyes quickly washed away. The colour became long associated with authority and status because of this highly prized Tyrian purple. The laborious manufacture of the dye, requiring tens of thousands of murex sea snails to supply enough pigment to colour a small swatch of fabric, meant it was worth more than its weight in gold.

The search for new supplies and new markets for their dye drove the Phoenicians onward, and by the 9th century BCE, the Phoenician empire had become one of the most powerful trading blocs in the world.

---

## The Colour of Emperors

Once the colour of Caesar's and Catholic cardinals' robes, purple was long associated with royalty and being "born to the purple." Roman emperors restricted who could wear purple — sometimes only the emperor himself. Roman emperors passed laws called "sumptuary laws" to control who could wear it. Only the emperor could wear a robe fully dyed in purple. Senators could wear a white toga with a single purple stripe. Priests used purple garments during sacred rituals.

The colour was so revered that it was strictly reserved for emperors and kings. In 40 AD, the King of Mauretania was assassinated on the orders of Caligula, and one rumour suggests that he dared to show up in Rome wearing a purple cloak.

Around 3,000 years ago, the Ancient Phoenicians had discovered how to make a rich purple dye that became more brilliant over time. Purple was worn exclusively by the upper class, and artists commissioned by the Catholic Church also depicted Jesus and the Virgin Mary in purple.

---

## The Fall of an Empire, the Loss of a Colour

Production of Tyrian purple for use as a fabric dye had begun as early as 1200 BC by the Phoenicians, and was continued by the Greeks and Romans until 1453 AD, with the fall of Constantinople. The Byzantine Empire, which controlled the dye trade, declined. The technique of making the dye was kept secret, passed down within families, and eventually lost. Cheaper dyes, like those made from plants, became more practical. By the time of the Renaissance, the original recipe for Tyrian purple was forgotten. People knew it once existed, but nobody knew how to make it anymore.

For centuries, the world's most powerful colour simply vanished.

---

## A Teenage Chemist and a Happy Accident

It wasn't until the 19th century that purple made a comeback. In 1856, an 18-year-old chemistry student named William Henry Perkin accidentally created the first synthetic purple dye while trying to make a medicine for malaria. He called it mauveine.

Perkin made several attempts at the synthesis over the Easter vacation in his home laboratory, using coal tar as a source of aniline. Oxidising the aniline with potassium dichromate gave a black sludge — but it contained something far more exciting. Perkin noticed whilst cleaning out a flask with ethanol that a purple solution had formed — an observation which led to Perkin becoming one of the most celebrated chemists of the Victorian era.

In the lab he'd set up in his parents' loft, he stained a piece of cloth in the brilliant purple solution he came up with after adding alcohol to the oily mess he'd created from the aniline in coal tar. He couldn't remove it by washing. He realised this colour, which "resisted the action of the atmosphere, light, and soap," had tremendous potential.

Perkin initially called his mauveine "Tyrian purple," deliberately referencing the ancient murex dye in order to give his synthetic dye greater market appeal. He soon switched to calling it mauve, after the French name for the mallow flower.

---

## Mauve Measles and a Fashion Revolution

This discovery brought purple — a colour so expensive it had previously only been afforded by royalty and the Church — to the mass market. Purple became the height of fashion in Paris and London in the late 1850s to early 1860s, and the frenzy over mauve became known as "mauveine measles." Even Queen Victoria was not exempt from the excitement, appearing in 1862 at the International Exhibition wearing a silk dress coloured by mauveine. The wife of Napoleon III, Empress Eugénie, wore mauveine-dyed dresses to state functions.

Perkin's purple dyestuff marked the beginning of a revolution in organic chemistry, the birth of an industry that has since given us a rainbow of colours, as well as drugs, explosives, fertilisers, plastics, and synthetics beyond measure. Perkin's mauve was also used
